evidence.title: Study of the failure of condenser tube in water cooled centrifugal chiller
evidence.abstract: Centrifugal Chiller is the most essential component of district cooling system. Intricate electromechanical design of the chiller leads to certain unanticipated and unpredictable failures, which affect the overall operational efficiency and reliability of the plant. A case study of unusual type of failure in centrifugal chiller serving district cooling plant has been discussed and presented in this paper. The main purpose of the study is to evaluate the underlying cause of failure of condenser tube. The study takes all possible failure assessments into consideration starting from visual inspection through hardness test, down to x-ray diffractometry. The end of the study demonstrates that the condenser tube leakage is principally attributed to impingement of miniature high velocity water jet at the small region inside the tube which removes the protective copper oxide film, thereby, making that area susceptible to corrosion. Entrapped vibrating foreign wire-like body with free end grinding against interior wall of the copper tube causes a similar damage to the protective film at the same area. Both effects resulted in a rarely reported type of erosion-corrosion phenomenon which finally causes the tube failure.

evidence.title: Effects of Pulse Frequency on Performance of Electrochemical Cooling  Water Treatment for Cooling Tower of Water-Cooled Chiller
evidence.abstract: Due to the rapid economic development in recent years, water-chiller is being used more and more in hotels, restaurants, resorts, and industrial zones in Vietnam. The cooling tower’s cooling water quality is an important factor in determining the effect on electrical consumption and the coefficient of performance of a water-cooled chiller. Therefore, it is necessary to maintain the quality of cooling water during the operation time of the water-cooled chiller. The aim of this work is to investigate the effects of the pulse frequency and operational parameters such as current density, pulse duty cycle, and energy consumption on the performance of removing hardness ion of electrochemical cooling water treatment for the cooling tower of the water-cooled chiller. The results show that the highest efficiency of the total hardness removal corresponding to a pulse frequency of 1 kHz, a pulse duty cycle of 0.7, and a current density of 80A/m2.

evidence.title: Reducing Cooling Tower Fill Fouling and Degradation With Water Quality Control
evidence.abstract: Cooling tower fill may be composed of wood or plastic, but it must provide adequate surface area for heat dissipation. Online and field water quality analysis can maximize tower efficiency and minimize maintenance. Uncontrolled levels of pH, bio-growth, or over-application of chemicals cause degradation of the material and plugging. Automatic control of pH conditioner can be accomplished with proven differential pH methods tied to analog and/or digital control. Oxidizing biocide application can be optimized with ORP and halogen analysis and control. Overuse of this type of biocide can also cause wood delignification that can affect the structural integrity of the tower. Another cause of fouling is excessive solids accumulation. Solids buildup can be minimized with side-stream filtration and/or clarification and monitored with low maintenance self-cleaning optical probes.

evidence.title: Design of Industrial Water Cooled Chiller for Recycle Cyclohexane in Polyethylene Plant
evidence.abstract: The research was aimed at providing water for cooling recycled cyclohexane in polyethylene plant to 15°C. This research could be redounding to the benefit of polyethylene plants that are using solution based polymerization technique. A chiller unit of 630 T, which has compressor power input of 378.33 kW and can provide chilled water capable of cooling recycle cyclohexane to 15°C, was designed using Aspen Hysys version 7.1. Four different refrigerants were tested to know the best fit refrigerant for the design and the best among them was R134a. The designed chiller has a coefficient of performance of 6.3 and a capacity greater than that of the defective chiller (550 TR). Unlike the defective chiller, with the increased cooling capacity and corresponding increase in compressor power from 296 kW to 378.6 kW, it could discharge chilled water capable of cooling recycle cyclohexane from 38°C to 15°C without tripping of the unit. With this design, ethylene absorption rate could increase to 40 T/h. Evaporator and condenser were designed and duties were 2166.39 KJ/sec and 2544.72 KJ/sec respectively. A thermostatic expansion valve with flow coefficient of 46.17 gpm was designed. The designed suction and discharge pressure were 414 kpa and 1053 kpa respectively while condenser temperature of 40°C was used for the design. The cooling of recycle cyclohexane from 38°C to 15°C using the chilled water supplied by the designed chiller was simulated using Aspen Hysys.

evidence.title: Performance Prediction of a Water-Cooled Centrifugal Chiller in Standard Temperature Conditions Using In-Situ Measurement Data
evidence.abstract: In this study, a regression model was developed using the thermo-regulated residual refinement regression model (TRRM) analysis method based on three years and four months of in situ data collected from two water-cooled centrifugal chillers installed in A Tower, Seoul, South Korea. The primary objective of this study was to predict the coefficient of performance (COP) of water-cooled chillers under various operating conditions using only the chilled water outlet temperature (T2) and the cooling water inlet temperature (T3). The secondary objective was to estimate the COP under standard temperature conditions, which is essential for the absolute performance evaluation of chillers. The collected dataset was refined through thermodynamic preprocessing, including the removal of missing values and outliers, to ensure high data reliability. Based on this refined dataset, regression analyses were conducted separately for four cases: daytime (09:00–21:00) and nighttime (21:00–09:00) operations of chiller #1 and chiller #2, resulting in the derivation of four final regression equations. The reliability of the final dataset was further validated by applying other regression models, including simple linear (SL), bi-quadratic (BQ), and multivariate polynomial (MP) regression. The performance of each model was evaluated by calculating the coefficient of determination (R2), coefficient of variation of root mean square error (CVRMSE), and the p-values of each coefficient. Additionally, the predicted COP values under the design and standard temperature conditions were compared with the measured COP values to assess the accuracy of the model. Error rates were also analyzed under scenarios where T2 and T3 were each varied by ±1 °C. To ensure robust validation, a final comparison was performed between the predicted and measured COP values. The results demonstrated that the TRRM exhibited high reliability and predictive accuracy, with most regression equations achieving R2 values exceeding 90%, CVRMSE below 5%, and p-values below 0.05. Furthermore, the predicted COP values closely matched the actual measured COP values, further confirming the reliability of the regression model and equations. evidence.title: Central cooling: compressive chillers
evidence.abstract: Representative cost and performance data are provided in a concise, useable form for three types of compressive liquid packaged chillers: reciprocating, centrifugal, and screw. The data are represented in graphical form as well as in empirical equations. Reciprocating chillers are available from 2.5 to 240 tons with full-load COPs ranging from 2.85 to 3.87. Centrifugal chillers are available from 80 to 2,000 tons with full load COPs ranging from 4.1 to 4.9. Field-assemblied centrifugal chillers have been installed with capacities up to 10,000 tons. Screw-type chillers are available from 100 to 750 tons with full load COPs ranging from 3.3 to 4.5.

mechanism_map.mechanism: Erosion-corrosion of condenser tubes caused by high-velocity water jet impingement and vibrating foreign wire-like bodies removing the protective copper oxide film
mechanism_map.intervention: Install a **dual-layer filtration system** with a **magnetic separator** upstream of the condenser tubes to remove suspended metallic debris (e.g., wire fragments) and a **vortex flow inducer** inside the tubes to disrupt high-velocity jet formation while maintaining flow velocity below the erosion threshold (~1.5 m/s for copper alloys)
mechanism_map.expected_effect: Reduction of erosion-corrosion damage to condenser tubes, preserving the protective copper oxide layer, thereby minimizing fouling-related condensing temperature rise and restoring plant capacity to within 2% of baseline at peak load
mechanism_map.falsification_test: Post-implementation inspection of 10% of condenser tubes via **borescope** after 12 months of operation should show <5% surface area with exposed copper (no oxide film) and <1 metallic foreign body per 100m of tubing, compared to pre-intervention baseline

system.value: Reducing Cooling Tower Fill Fouling and Degradation With Water Quality Control

abstract.value: Cooling tower fill may be composed of wood or plastic, but it must provide adequate surface area for heat dissipation. Online and field water quality analysis can maximize tower efficiency and minimize maintenance. Uncontrolled levels of pH, bio-growth, or over-application of chemicals cause degradation of the material and plugging. Automatic control of pH conditioner can be accomplished with proven differential pH methods tied to analog and/or digital control. Oxidizing biocide application can be optimized with ORP and halogen analysis and control. Overuse of this type of biocide can also cause wood delignification that can affect the structural integrity of the tower. Another cause of fouling is excessive solids accumulation. Solids buildup can be minimized with side-stream filtration and/or clarification and monitored with low maintenance self-cleaning optical probes.

system.value: Design of Industrial Water Cooled Chiller for Recycle Cyclohexane in Polyethylene Plant

abstract.value: The research was aimed at providing water for cooling recycled cyclohexane in polyethylene plant to 15°C. This research could be redounding to the benefit of polyethylene plants that are using solution based polymerization technique. A chiller unit of 630 T, which has compressor power input of 378.33 kW and can provide chilled water capable of cooling recycle cyclohexane to 15°C, was designed using Aspen Hysys version 7.1. Four different refrigerants were tested to know the best fit refrigerant for the design and the best among them was R134a. The designed chiller has a coefficient of performance of 6.3 and a capacity greater than that of the defective chiller (550 TR). Unlike the defective chiller, with the increased cooling capacity and corresponding increase in compressor power from 296 kW to 378.6 kW, it could discharge chilled water capable of cooling recycle cyclohexane from 38°C to 15°C without tripping of the unit. With this design, ethylene absorption rate could increase to 40 T/h. Evaporator and condenser were designed and duties were 2166.39 KJ/sec and 2544.72 KJ/sec respectively. A thermostatic expansion valve with flow coefficient of 46.17 gpm was designed. The designed suction and discharge pressure were 414 kpa and 1053 kpa respectively while condenser temperature of 40°C was used for the design. The cooling of recycle cyclohexane from 38°C to 15°C using the chilled water supplied by the designed chiller was simulated using Aspen Hysys.

system.value: Performance Prediction of a Water-Cooled Centrifugal Chiller in Standard Temperature Conditions Using In-Situ Measurement Data

abstract.value: In this study, a regression model was developed using the thermo-regulated residual refinement regression model (TRRM) analysis method based on three years and four months of in situ data collected from two water-cooled centrifugal chillers installed in A Tower, Seoul, South Korea. The primary objective of this study was to predict the coefficient of performance (COP) of water-cooled chillers under various operating conditions using only the chilled water outlet temperature (T2) and the cooling water inlet temperature (T3). The secondary objective was to estimate the COP under standard temperature conditions, which is essential for the absolute performance evaluation of chillers. The collected dataset was refined through thermodynamic preprocessing, including the removal of missing values and outliers, to ensure high data reliability. Based on this refined dataset, regression analyses were conducted separately for four cases: daytime (09:00–21:00) and nighttime (21:00–09:00) operations of chiller #1 and chiller #2, resulting in the derivation of four final regression equations. The reliability of the final dataset was further validated by applying other regression models, including simple linear (SL), bi-quadratic (BQ), and multivariate polynomial (MP) regression. The performance of each model was evaluated by calculating the coefficient of determination (R2), coefficient of variation of root mean square error (CVRMSE), and the p-values of each coefficient. Additionally, the predicted COP values under the design and standard temperature conditions were compared with the measured COP values to assess the accuracy of the model. Error rates were also analyzed under scenarios where T2 and T3 were each varied by ±1 °C. To ensure robust validation, a final comparison was performed between the predicted and measured COP values. The results demonstrated that the TRRM exhibited high reliability and predictive accuracy, with most regression equations achieving R2 values exceeding 90%, CVRMSE below 5%, and p-values below 0.05. Furthermore, the predicted COP values closely matched the actual measured COP values, further confirming the reliability of the regression model and equations. This study provides a practical method for estimating the COP of water-cooled chillers under standard temperature conditions or other operational conditions using only T2 and T3. This meth

abstract.value: Representative cost and performance data are provided in a concise, useable form for three types of compressive liquid packaged chillers: reciprocating, centrifugal, and screw. The data are represented in graphical form as well as in empirical equations. Reciprocating chillers are available from 2.5 to 240 tons with full-load COPs ranging from 2.85 to 3.87. Centrifugal chillers are available from 80 to 2,000 tons with full load COPs ranging from 4.1 to 4.9. Field-assemblied centrifugal chillers have been installed with capacities up to 10,000 tons. Screw-type chillers are available from 100 to 750 tons with full load COPs ranging from 3.3 to 4.5.

candidates.mechanism: **Erosion-corrosion from high-velocity water jet impingement** — Miniature high-velocity water jets (e.g., from turbulent flow or misaligned spray nozzles) locally remove the protective copper oxide film on condenser tubes, exposing bare copper to corrosion and fouling. The combined effect of mechanical erosion and chemical corrosion accelerates scale deposition in the denuded zone, raising condensing temperature and reducing heat transfer efficiency.
candidates.intervention: **Install low-turbulence flow distributors** — Replace existing tube-side water distribution manifolds with **swirl-free, laminar-flow inlet nozzles** (e.g., helical or vortex-dampening designs) to eliminate high-velocity jet impingement zones. Add **internal baffles** in the water box to homogenize flow velocity across all tubes (<1.5 m/s max at inlet).

cemetery_warnings.lesson:
FROZEN THEOREM CE-018: A novelty claim survives only when the candidate's CAPABILITY (what it can DO) is demonstrably absent from the prior art landscape — not when the candidate's KEYWORDS (what words it uses) are absent. The correct procedure: (1) decompose the candidate into its functional capabilities (e.g., 'intrapprocedural clot sensing' not 'retrieved-clot physical signature measurement'); (2) search the prior art landscape for each capability using the prior art's own vocabulary (assignee names, CPC classes, commercial product names, inventor terminology); (3) build a capability collision matrix mapping each capability to prior art coverage; (4) only if at least one capability is genuinely UNOCCUPIED (confirmed by both patent search AND commercial frontier analysis) can a novelty claim be recorded. Semantic re-skins (CE-012 violation) include: 'retrieved-clot' vs 'in-situ clot'; 'physical signature' vs 'composition'; 'integrated sensor' vs 'catheter-mounted sensor.' These distinctions prove nothing. The test is capability, not vocabulary.

SHARPENED (per CEO Round 62 audit): Capability novelty must be evaluated at the FUNCTIONAL END-TO-END level: input → inference → decision → physical effect → measurable outcome. A 'novel' intermediate layer that plugs into an existing end-to-end system is NOT novel — it is a substitution, not an invention. The unit of novelty is the complete causal loop, not the sensor, feature, algorithm, or capability.

cemetery_warnings.mechanism: Capability collision test — keyword collision search is insufficient to establish novelty
cemetery_warnings.lesson:
FROZEN THEOREM CE-018: A novelty claim survives only when the candidate's CAPABILITY (what it can DO) is demonstrably absent from the prior art landscape — not when the candidate's KEYWORDS (what words it uses) are absent. The correct procedure: (1) decompose the candidate into its functional capabilities (e.g., 'intrapprocedural clot sensing' not 'retrieved-clot physical signature measurement'); (2) search the prior art landscape for each capability using the prior art's own vocabulary (assignee names, CPC classes, commercial product names, inventor terminology); (3) build a capability collision matrix mapping each capability to prior art coverage; (4) only if at least one capability is genuinely UNOCCUPIED (confirmed by both patent search AND commercial frontier analysis) can a novelty claim be recorded. Semantic re-skins (CE-012 violation) include: 'retrieved-clot' vs 'in-situ clot'; 'physical signature' vs 'composition'; 'integrated sensor' vs 'catheter-mounted sensor.' These distinctions prove nothing. The test is capability, not vocabulary.

SHARPENED (per CEO Round 62 audit): Capability novelty must be evaluated at the FUNCTIONAL END-TO-END level: input → inference → decision → physical effect → measurable outcome. Otherwise the machine can still find a 'novel' intermediate layer (e.g., a new sensor modality, a new feature, a new algorithm) that is already covered by an existing end-to-end system. The correct end-to-end test: (5) decompose the candidate into the complete causal loop — what is observed → what is inferred → what is predicted → what physical action becomes possible → what measurable outcome changes; (6) map each step of this loop to the prior art's end-to-end systems (not just individual capabilities); (7) only if the candidate's complete causal loop is demonstrably absent from the prior art's end-to-end systems can a novelty claim be recorded. A 'novel' intermediate layer that plugs into an existing end-to-end system is NOT novel — it is a substitution, not an invention. The unit of novelty is the complete causal loop, not the sensor, feature, algorithm, or capability.

The combined effect of mechanical erosion and chemical corrosion accelerates scale deposition in the denuded zone, raising condensing temperature and reducing heat transfer efficiency.
candidates.intervention: **Install low-turbulence flow distributors** — Replace existing tube-side water distribution manifolds with **swirl-free, laminar-flow inlet nozzles** (e.g., helical or vortex-dampening designs) to eliminate high-velocity jet impingement zones. Add **internal baffles** in the water box to homogenize flow velocity across all tubes (<1.5 m/s max at inlet).

hypothesis_attribution.mechanism: **Erosion-corrosion from high-velocity water jet impingement** — Miniature high-velocity water jets (e.g., from turbulent flow or misaligned spray nozzles) locally remove the protective copper oxide film on condenser tubes, exposing bare copper to corrosion and fouling. The combined effect of mechanical erosion and chemical corrosion accelerates scale deposition in the denuded zone, raising condensing temperature and reducing heat transfer efficiency.
hypothesis_attribution.intervention: **Install low-turbulence flow distributors** — Replace existing tube-side water distribution manifolds with **swirl-free, laminar-flow inlet nozzles** (e.g., helical or vortex-dampening designs) to eliminate high-velocity jet impingement zones. Add **internal baffles** in the water box to homogenize flow velocity across all tubes (<1.5 m/s max at inlet).

hypothesis_attribution.mechanism: **Vibration-induced erosion from entrained foreign bodies** — Wire-like debris (e.g., corroded metal fragments, fiberglass strands) entrained in cooling tower water vibrates against the interior tube wall at resonant frequencies (aligned with chiller pump flow pulsations), mechanically abrading the copper oxide layer. The resulting localized denudation initiates **erosion-corrosion pits**, which act as nucleation sites for scale deposition and further reduce heat transfer.
hypothesis_attribution.intervention: **Magnetic + mesh hybrid filter array** — Install a **two-stage filtration system** at the condenser water inlet: (1) **Permanent magnet grid** (to capture ferromagnetic debris) followed by (2) **300-mesh stainless steel screen** (to trap non-metallic fibers >100 µm). Add **acoustic vibration dampers** (tuned to chiller pump frequencies) on the water box to suppress debris-induced tube wall excitation.

hypothesis_attribution.mechanism: **Chemical fouling amplification in erosion-corrosion zones** — The mechanical removal of the copper oxide film (via jet impingement or abrasion) disrupts the passive corrosion barrier, locally increasing the **copper dissolution rate** in the presence of chlorides/sulfates. The dissolved copper ions then **catalyze scale precipitation** (e.g., CaCO₃, Mg(OH)₂) in the denuded zones, forming dense, thermally insulating deposits that accelerate condensing temperature rise.
hypothesis_attribution.intervention: **Electrochemical protection with sacrificial anodes** — Install **zinc-aluminum alloy sacrificial anodes** (coupled to the copper tubes via insulated connections) inside the condenser water box. Supplement with **periodic low-voltage pulsed current (LVPPC)** (50 mA/m², 100 ms pulses every 5 min) to reinforce oxide film repair in high-risk zones. Monitor anode dissolution rate via weight loss sensors.

hypothesis_attribution.mechanism: **Domain knowledge (fluid dynamics) + Evidence (erosion-corrosion):** High-velocity water jets impinging on localized regions of the condenser tube remove the protective copper oxide film, initiating erosion-corrosion. The mechanism is driven by turbulent flow patterns and foreign body vibration, both of which disrupt the oxide layer, exposing the base metal to corrosive attack. The causal chain is: **turbulence → localized high-velocity impingement → oxide film removal → localized corrosion → tube failure**.
hypothesis_attribution.intervention: **Install helical internal fins or spiral grooves inside the condenser tubes** to disrupt large-scale turbulent flow structures and redistribute water velocity uniformly along the tube length. The helical geometry forces the water to follow a helical path, reducing localized high-velocity jets and mitigating erosion-corrosion at fixed points.

hypothesis_attribution.mechanism: **Domain knowledge (vibration-induced wear) + Evidence (foreign body grinding):** Entrapped vibrating wire-like debris acts as a high-frequency abrasive, grinding against the tube interior and mechanically removing the copper oxide film. The mechanism is: **vibration amplitude → debris impact energy → localized oxide film abrasion → corrosion initiation → tube perforation**. The causal link is supported by the record’s observation of "entrapped vibrating foreign wire-like body."
hypothesis_attribution.intervention: **Introduce a magnetic filter assembly upstream of the condenser tubes** to capture ferromagnetic debris (e.g., wire fragments, metal particles) before they enter the tube bundle. The filter uses an array of rare-earth magnets (NdFeB) with a 0.5 mm clearance gap to trap debris while allowing water flow.

hypothesis_attribution.mechanism: **Domain knowledge (corrosion science) + Evidence (oxide film removal):** The protective copper oxide (Cu₂O/CuO) layer is selectively removed in high-velocity zones, creating galvanic microcells between bare copper and oxidized regions. The mechanism is: **localized oxide removal → differential aeration → galvanic corrosion → pitting → tube failure**. The record’s evidence confirms that oxide film removal is the critical trigger.

The coating is electrically insulating but permeable to heat, preserving thermal performance while preventing galvanic coupling between bare copper and oxidized areas.

By modifying the internal tube geometry to disrupt laminar flow and promote turbulent flow, the effective heat transfer coefficient is increased, counteracting the fouling-induced resistance.

CROSS_DOMAIN_MIN_NONGENERIC_OVERLAP.justification: R377 patent-text ground truth (TOSCANINI/R377_PATENT_TEXT_FETCH.json + R377_PATENT_TEXT_GROUND_TRUTH.json): 12/30 family representatives (40%) were substantively irrelevant cross-domain term collisions (CWDM optical link for a battery-thermal candidate; dental-condition monitoring for rolling stock; bone fracture forceps for rail steel...). A hit sharing NO entity term with the candidate now needs >= 3 NON-generic mechanism terms to be mechanism art: the measured true cross-domain analog (line-pipe steel with hydrogen fracture toughness for a rail-steel candidate) shares 3 non-generic terms and survives; every measured false positive shares <= 2 and is demoted. This RAISES the cross-domain bar (was the same >= 2 as same-domain) — stricter, not weaker (Art. VII).
CROSS_DOMAIN_MIN_NONGENERIC_OVERLAP.uncertainty: term overlap remains a proxy; entity word-sense collisions ('gear': steering vs draft) can still pass — disclosed limitation, not a solved problem

MIN_MECHANISM_OVERLAP.justification: same term-overlap rule family as the pipeline relevance adjudicator and the Q2 instrument (>= 2 shared content terms = domain-specific rather than accidental collision); NOT weakened relative to any prior gate
MIN_MECHANISM_OVERLAP.uncertainty: term overlap is a proxy for mechanism identity

ANTICIPATION_COVERAGE_RATIO.justification: a family ANTICIPATES only when nearly ALL elements of the candidate's FULL distinguishing set (uncapped — the claim elements, not the 6-term query core) appear in the family's claim/abstract text; 0.8 leaves a >= 20% element margin — anything lower would convert partial art into a kill (Art. XXVIII forbids). Measured adversarial case: a domain-only patent reached 0.857 against a capped denominator whose true differentiators (acoustic, multi-modal) had been ranked out
ANTICIPATION_COVERAGE_RATIO.uncertainty: claim coverage measured by term overlap, not a claim chart; recorded per family with evidence tier

MAX_QUERY_TERMS.justification: provider-measured sweet spot for keyword patent queries (longer queries dilute ranking)

ABSTRACT_TIER_MIN_CHARS.justification: below ~80 chars a snippet carries title echoes, not mechanism description; it cannot support an abstract-tier coverage decision

custody_records.raw_content: Centrifugal Chiller is the most essential component of district cooling system. Intricate electromechanical design of the chiller leads to certain unanticipated and unpredictable failures, which affect the overall operational efficiency and reliability of the plant. A case study of unusual type of failure in centrifugal chiller serving district cooling plant has been discussed and presented in this paper. The main purpose of the study is to evaluate the underlying cause of failure of condenser tube. The study takes all possible failure assessments into consideration starting from visual inspection through hardness test, down to x-ray diffractometry. The end of the study demonstrates that the condenser tube leakage is principally attributed to impingement of miniature high velocity water jet at the small region inside the tube which removes the protective copper oxide film, thereby, making that area susceptible to corrosion. Entrapped vibrating foreign wire-like body with free end grinding against interior wall of the copper tube causes a similar damage to the protective film at the same area. Both effects resulted in a rarely reported type of erosion-corrosion phenomenon which finally causes the tube failure.

custody_records.raw_content: Due to the rapid economic development in recent years, water-chiller is being used more and more in hotels, restaurants, resorts, and industrial zones in Vietnam. The cooling tower’s cooling water quality is an important factor in determining the effect on electrical consumption and the coefficient of performance of a water-cooled chiller. Therefore, it is necessary to maintain the quality of cooling water during the operation time of the water-cooled chiller. The aim of this work is to investigate the effects of the pulse frequency and operational parameters such as current density, pulse duty cycle, and energy consumption on the performance of removing hardness ion of electrochemical cooling water treatment for the cooling tower of the water-cooled chiller. The results show that the highest efficiency of the total hardness removal corresponding to a pulse frequency of 1 kHz, a pulse duty cycle of 0.7, and a current density of 80A/m2.

custody_records.raw_content: Cooling tower fill may be composed of wood or plastic, but it must provide adequate surface area for heat dissipation. Online and field water quality analysis can maximize tower efficiency and minimize maintenance. Uncontrolled levels of pH, bio-growth, or over-application of chemicals cause degradation of the material and plugging. Automatic control of pH conditioner can be accomplished with proven differential pH methods tied to analog and/or digital control. Oxidizing biocide application can be optimized with ORP and halogen analysis and control. Overuse of this type of biocide can also cause wood delignification that can affect the structural integrity of the tower. Another cause of fouling is excessive solids accumulation. Solids buildup can be minimized with side-stream filtration and/or clarification and monitored with low maintenance self-cleaning optical probes.

Submitted as a formal supplemental comment and technical basis for public rulemaking before the Public Utility Commission of Texas (PUCT), GRUS-STD-60084 v2.0 provides the first standardized, vendor-neutral methodology designed to bridge the fatal gaps exposed by self-reporting failures under state surveys and executive audit directives.  Following the Governor’s Directive of August 3, 2026, mandating comprehensive verification of the massive ERCOT interconnection queue (~474 GW, ~90% data-center driven), and implementing requirements under Senate Bill 6 (PURA § 37.0561), this document establishes that resource consumption cannot be left to unverified self-assertions by facility operators.  Key Architectural ComponentsThe Two-Meter Water Method (§ V.A): Establishes a rigorous, non-fictional water accounting framework utilizing a primary property-entrance master meter alongside a secondary point-of-use submeter on all evaporative circuits (cooling towers, misting/adiabatic assists, and on-site generation cooling), isolating consumptive loss to atmosphere from returned blowdown to safeguard municipal infrastructure and ensure compliance with state pressure floors (30 TAC §§ 290.44(d), 290.46(r)).  The Two-Tier Electrical Transport Boundary (§ V.D): Moves measurement past the facility fence (M1) to the internal transport boundary (M2) at the power distribution unit (PDU) level, utilizing ANSI C12.20 / IEC 62053-22 revenue-grade submeters combined with open native server telemetry (DMTF Redfish, IPMI) to capture high-amplitude volatile peaks without inspecting proprietary algorithms or tenant data.  The Two-Axis Classification Framework (Part IV): Categorizes facilities by Workload Profile (W-1 Continuous, W-2 Burst, W-3 Mixed) and Cooling Method (C-1 Air through C-5 Generation-Cooling), incorporating an automatic reclassification trigger whenever d

custody_records.raw_content: The research was aimed at providing water for cooling recycled cyclohexane in polyethylene plant to 15°C. This research could be redounding to the benefit of polyethylene plants that are using solution based polymerization technique. A chiller unit of 630 T, which has compressor power input of 378.33 kW and can provide chilled water capable of cooling recycle cyclohexane to 15°C, was designed using Aspen Hysys version 7.1. Four different refrigerants were tested to know the best fit refrigerant for the design and the best among them was R134a. The designed chiller has a coefficient of performance of 6.3 and a capacity greater than that of the defective chiller (550 TR). Unlike the defective chiller, with the increased cooling capacity and corresponding increase in compressor power from 296 kW to 378.6 kW, it could discharge chilled water capable of cooling recycle cyclohexane from 38°C to 15°C without tripping of the unit. With this design, ethylene absorption rate could increase to 40 T/h. Evaporator and condenser were designed and duties were 2166.39 KJ/sec and 2544.72 KJ/sec respectively. A thermostatic expansion valve with flow coefficient of 46.17 gpm was designed. The designed suction and discharge pressure were 414 kpa and 1053 kpa respectively while condenser temperature of 40°C was used for the design. The cooling of recycle cyclohexane from 38°C to 15°C using the chilled water supplied by the designed chiller was simulated using Aspen Hysys.

custody_records.raw_content: In this study, a regression model was developed using the thermo-regulated residual refinement regression model (TRRM) analysis method based on three years and four months of in situ data collected from two water-cooled centrifugal chillers installed in A Tower, Seoul, South Korea. The primary objective of this study was to predict the coefficient of performance (COP) of water-cooled chillers under various operating conditions using only the chilled water outlet temperature (T2) and the cooling water inlet temperature (T3). The secondary objective was to estimate the COP under standard temperature conditions, which is essential for the absolute performance evaluation of chillers. The collected dataset was refined through thermodynamic preprocessing, including the removal of missing values and outliers, to ensure high data reliability. Based on this refined dataset, regression analyses were conducted separately for four cases: daytime (09:00–21:00) and nighttime (21:00–09:00) operations of chiller #1 and chiller #2, resulting in the derivation of four final regression equations. The reliability of the final dataset was further validated by applying other regression models, including simple linear (SL), bi-quadratic (BQ), and multivariate polynomial (MP) regression. The performance of each model was evaluated by calculating the coefficient of determination (R2), coefficient of variation of root mean square error (CVRMSE), and the p-values of each coefficient. Additionally, the predicted COP values under the design and standard temperature conditions were compared with the measured COP values to assess the accuracy of the model. Error rates were also analyzed under scenarios where T2 and T3 were each varied by ±1 °C. To ensure robust validation, a final comparison was performed between the predicted and measured COP values. The results demonstrated that the TRRM exhibited high reliability and predictive accuracy, with most regression equations achieving R2 values exceeding 90%, CVRMSE below 5%, and p-values below 0.05. Furthermore, the predicted COP values closely matched the actual measured COP values, further confirming the reliability of the regression model and equations. custody_records.raw_content: Representative cost and performance data are provided in a concise, useable form for three types of compressive liquid packaged chillers: reciprocating, centrifugal, and screw. The data are represented in graphical form as well as in empirical equations. Reciprocating chillers are available from 2.5 to 240 tons with full-load COPs ranging from 2.85 to 3.87. Centrifugal chillers are available from 80 to 2,000 tons with full load COPs ranging from 4.1 to 4.9. Field-assemblied centrifugal chillers have been installed with capacities up to 10,000 tons. Screw-type chillers are available from 100 to 750 tons with full load COPs ranging from 3.3 to 4.5.
